China's 800MW AI campus takes on Stargate with wind power, batteries and 800V DC

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China is building an 800MW AI data center campus in Inner Mongolia that could challenge the economics of America's Stargate project, according to a new report from SemiAnalysis. Envision has built the first 120 MW of Galaxy AI data center campus in less than a year, a cost the researchers put at just one-fifth of comparable US projects, after visiting the site in September.

But getting the buildings up is only half of the battle. AI data centers need enormous amounts of electricity, and Envision is taking an unusual route to secure it— building its own wind farms and battery storage alongside the computing facility.

While US developers are turning to on-site gas turbines to work around grid constraints, Envision is building its data center alongside wind farms, battery storage, and dedicated power infrastructure. Galaxy is located in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, and is being developed across four phases for two unnamed internet companies. The completed campus is planned to provide up to 800MW of IT capacity by the end of 2027, putting it closer to the approximately 820MW of critical IT capacity at the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas.

Envision is building its own power supply for Galaxy rather than leaving everything to the local grid. So far, the company has installed more than 100GW of wind turbines and wants its wind farms to provide over 60% of the electricity needed by the campus’s first two phases. Those farms, located about 80 kilometers apart, have a combined capacity of 420MW. That's well above the 240MW load expected from the first two phases, although wind turbines rarely get to run flat out. Ulanqab’s wind capacity factor is between 355 and 40%, so Envision is adding four-hour battery storage to keep the electricity coming when the wind dies down.

Power equipment is proving rather hard to come by for some US data center builders. We have previously reported on turbine shortages that have pushed delivery estimates to 2030, while SpaceX is looking to manufacture its own turbine blades for its gas-powered AI facilities. Envision, meanwhile, is putting wind generation and battery storage right alongside its servers.

The power hardware inside the Galaxy is worth a look, too. Semianalyss visited a 5MW hall where solid-state transformers take 10kV AC electricity and convert it directly into 800V DC for the server racks. That's a fairly substantial departure from conventional data-center power distribution, which typically involves several intermediate conversion stages. “In one 5MW hall, we saw the 800V system at work,” the researchers wrote. They explained that “Solid-state transformers (SSTs) take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks.”

The design removes several intermediate components found in conventional data center power systems, including low voltage transformers, uninterruptible power supplies and rectifiers. Fewer conversion stages can reduce equipment requirements and energy losses, although SemiAnalysis did not provide a measured efficiency improvement for Galaxy’s pilot. The 5MW installation is only a small part of the campus, but it puts the technology into operation at a live facility. Envision, however, plans an even larger deployment in the next construction phases, a move that aligns with Nvidia's push for 800V DC distribution in future high-density AI systems.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Galaxy's campus uses a cooling arrangement in which liquid-cooled and air-cooled servers share a single water loop, eliminating the need for conventional central chiller plants. That matters as AI servers generate more heat and require increasingly sophisticated cooling systems. Removing central chillers can simplify infrastructure, although the design depends on local climate conditions and the facility's ability to reject heat through its water loop. China has previously experimented with other unconventional cooling methods, including a wind-powered underwater datacenter off Shanghai that uses surrounding seawater to help cool its servers.

That said, Galaxy is the first major project in Invision's wider Inner Mongolia datacentre plans, which Semianalysis says add up to 3GW, with the rest of the campus still a busy construction site. The surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone is also expanding rapidly, with nearly 30,000 construction workers spread across 22 data center projects, according to a local report cited by the researchers.

The wider Chinese expansion is also attracting some of the world's largest technology companies. Alibaba, Huawei and ByteDance are among the firms expanding infrastructure in the region, which benefits from relatively cheap electricity, available land and abundant wind resources. However access to electricity and datacenter buildings does not automatically translate to available AI computing power. China's access to advanced accelerators remains a separate constraint, particularly as US export restrictions limit its ability to acquire Nvidia’s most powerful chips.

#10645. This Googlebook is driving me crazy

Right now, Googlebooks make more sense for Google than they do for users.

After trying for years to bring Android features to Chromebooks, Google decided to start over with Android as the foundation for a new laptop operating system. The first wave of Googlebooks are high-end laptops (priced $900 and up), with Google pitching them as the ultimate computers for Android enthusiasts.

But in their current form, Googlebooks are a disjointed mess, with websites and apps that don’t work quite right and AI features that aren’t fully fleshed out. While having a single operating system and app platform across laptops and mobile devices might make life easier for Google, it doesn’t yet translate to a better experience than the Chromebooks that Google aims to replace.

Android’s not ready for laptops

For the past month I’ve been using Acer’s Googlebook 14, which is the cheapest Googlebook at $900, and the only one whose touchscreen flips around into tablet mode. I have no major complaints about the hardware, which has a featherweight 2.51-pound chassis, a rich 120 Hz 3K OLED screen, and a smooth trackpad (albeit a “diving board” type whose click mechanism stiffens at the top edge).

My frustrations are more on the software side, where Android isn’t ready to carry a real laptop workload.

While Google is pushing developers to optimize their Android apps for large screens, keyboards, and trackpads, Google itself hasn’t always bothered to do so. The preloaded version of Gmail, for instance, is not an optimized Android app, but rather a web-based desktop app powered by the Chrome browser. Same goes for Google Docs, Drive, Meet, and YouTube. Tapping the menu button in these apps reveals a “Running in Chrome” disclaimer, and any Chrome extensions you install will apply to these apps as well.

This wouldn’t be a major concern if the web apps worked the way they’re supposed to. In Gmail, though, cursor hover controls don’t work, so you can’t quickly trash or archive messages line by line in the inbox. In Google Drive, documents open in a Chrome browser tab, while the same documents open in their own windows via Google Docs or Sheets. And if you try to select text in Google Docs using the touchscreen, the comment button pops up directly over the right text selector, making it unreachable.

Third-party Android apps can also have issues. Signing into Slack bounces me out to a Chrome tab, which then fails to authenticate back inside the Android app, so the only way to gain access is by manually entering a URL and password for each workplace. Even then, Slack’s Android app is poorly optimized, without the desktop version’s persistent sidebar.

Video apps still feel unfinished on Googlebooks as well. Those that Google deems “optimized for desktop,” such as Netflix and Disney+, will automatically open in full screen, which is jarring but at least fits the use case of watching video. Others, such as Fox One and NFL, open in a floating desktop window, and clicking their full screen icons accomplishes nothing. You’re actually supposed to ignore that button, highlight the maximize button in the window controls, then click the little “Full Screen” icon. Optimized or not, none of these apps support always-visible picture-in-picture mode like their mobile counterparts.

One last nitpick, admittedly a niche one: Bookmarklets don’t work on Googlebooks. I keep more than dozen of these in my browser’s address bar, which allows me to launch site-specific searches, create page excerpts, find archived versions of web pages, and remove “sticky” page elements. Not being able to use them on the Googlebook is a reminder that you’re not quite getting a full Chrome desktop experience.

The app situation will likely improve over time. When I started using the Googlebook, it wouldn’t let me install the Bluesky app and directed me to the web version. Now the app is available. Google Docs has also gained the ability to mark individual documents for offline use, which wasn’t possible at the outset. The Google Play Store has a tiered labeling system—“Optimized for Desktop,” “Compatible with Desktop,” “Better on the Website”—so you know what to expect, but for now the ecosystem is a work in progress.

Android synergies in progress

Googlebooks do have some neat features for Android users, the best of which is being able to access your phone’s files directly through the laptop’s Files app. There’s also “cross-device continuity,” which doesn’t work with many apps, but lets you quickly continue editing a message in Gmail or a document in Google Docs after opening it up on your phone.

App casting is rougher. If you have a phone running Android 17, this lets you view your phone’s apps through a Googlebook without installing them, and while this might be useful in some scenarios, it’s a subpar experience with jerky scrolling and occasional formatting issues. It can also lead to annoyances, like when a phone notification pops up on the Googlebook, and tapping it takes you into the janky app-casting version instead of the one that’s installed on your computer.

Android as a desktop operating system will also inherently pose some limitations. AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude lack the device control and folder-based file permissions that their desktop apps offer, and there are no command bar apps akin to Raycast for Windows and MacOS. The relative simplicity of an Android-based laptop may be a positive for some, but for me it’s a hindrance.

Too many Geminis

Beyond just catering to Android enthusiasts, Google is pitching Googlebooks as a premier surface for its Gemini AI assistant. In practice this means there are four main ways to invoke Gemini from the computer:

  • Wiggling your mouse cursor
  • Saying “Hey Google”
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the dock
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the Chrome taskbar

While having many entry points to Gemini makes sense, the execution feels disjointed. If you open the full Gemini app while a pop-up chat window is already open, for instance, the chat window closes and the full app cuts off your conversation, switching to a new one. The Chrome sidebar and pop-up window are also separate, so conversations in one don’t carry over to the other.

Those little inconsistencies tripped me up constantly, as I’d have to keep careful track of which conversation was happening where based on how I’d originally invoked it. Instead of just cramming AI touch points into different parts of the operating system, Google needs to do a better job of tying them all together.

There’s also a missed opportunity for Gemini to act more as an AI agent. While desktop AI apps on other platforms can work directly with files and folders on your computer, that’s currently not possible with Gemini on Googlebooks.

What’s next for Googlebooks?

Even if Googlebooks don’t feel ready now, they carry an air of inevitability. Google has already indicated that it will phase out Chrome OS by 2034, and it has outlined some vague plans for existing Chromebooks to turn into Googlebooks. Presumably that means Googlebooks will move down-market over time to include the kind of lower-end machines that defined the Chromebook business.

In the meantime, the question is whether Google will sufficiently invest in Googlebooks to address their weaknesses, instead of letting the project languish as it so often does (see: Stadia, Reader, its many attempts at social networking). One reason GoogleBooks feel so unpolished right now is because of Google’s hot-and-cold relationship with Android tablets, leading to a lack of app developer buy-in on devices with larger screens. With Google, there’s always a risk that it gets distracted by the next shiny object and leaves important work undone.

You can see how Googlebooks might eventually make sense: Combine a desktop-class Chrome experience with true Android app support, with easily available AI to help with research and automation. Maybe Google will get there someday, but first it needs to get more of the basics right.

#10643. Ray-Ban Meta Audio review: Great specs, shame about the price

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses attempt to curb the controversy by removing the cameras, and while they’re still an excellent product, the price makes them harder to recommend.

This has been a bit of a rollercoaster year for Meta wearables. Meta’s VR division shrank considerably earlier this year, then later announced a massively redesigned follow-up that’ll launch next year. And while Meta has debuted dozens of new smart glasses styles throughout the year that have sold quite well, the company can’t seem to get away from controversy. That’s where Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses come in.

Now, that doesn’t mean Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses aren’t worthwhile. They feature a much wider prescription range (-12 to +6) than the majority of Meta smart glasses models, which often cap out at -6 to +6. The battery life is also significantly better thanks to the lack of a camera and other improvements in the hardware. And, of course, if you want a pair of AI glasses but don’t want the camera, these are the only options from Meta.

If I were to choose between the two available models, I’d pick the Clubmaster style every time. Not only do they look better overall and feature the thinnest frames of any Meta smart glasses, but they also have substantially better nosepads that are adjustable and can be easily replaced.

The Burbank model looks just fine, but the nosepads aren’t the same, and the glasses feel more rigid overall (which I find less comfortable). Both models come in lots of colors with many different lens options, including clear, tinted, polarized, Transitions, and prescription.

Both models feature a touchpad on the outside of the right temple arm, as well as a small, circular button up top to activate Meta AI. You can alternatively use the “Hey, Meta” keywords to activate Meta AI. The button and touchpad can be disabled if you like. Only the touchpad has an alternative function, and that alternative function only controls music playback via Spotify or Amazon Music. Other Meta glasses offer far more options.

Both styles are the lightest Meta glasses available. Most Meta smart glasses with cameras weigh in around the 54g mark. Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses weigh just 44g. They’re not as light as Even Realities G2, RayNeo iO, or MemoMind One, but 44g is still considered pretty light for smart glasses.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses reuse the case from Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2, which looks more like a traditional Ray-Ban case rather than the foldable one that ships with Meta Ray-Ban Display or the 2026 Meta Camera Glasses. I don’t have an issue with Ray-Ban Meta Audio’s case at all, but I really enjoy the foldable one and wish it were included.

Audio playback on these is great, and while the speakers are identical to all other Meta glasses products, using them as spatial surround sound “headphones” while watching a movie with surround sound is a fantastic experience. They also have spatial audio recording and truly excellent noise cancellation thanks to the 6-mic setup.

But the lack of the newer processor from Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 means the glasses don’t support the new hearing aid function. To me, that’s a massive missed opportunity since these are audio-only glasses. When I asked Meta about it, they only said it wasn’t available on Ray-Ban Meta Audio for now, so this problem could be fixed in an upcoming update.

And that’s actually where Meta’s glasses might shine brightest: software updates. The company has been exemplary with update cadence on all of its products, and its smart glasses constantly get new, innovative features that surprise and delight. While I’m a little underwhelmed with the number of features available on these glasses today, this product will likely look quite different a year from now, a fact that’s backed up by years of Meta significantly improving product feature sets over time.

If you buy these glasses today, know that you’re mainly investing in them for the future. They’re fine enough for today’s usage, especially if you’re interested in a hands-free way to use Meta AI products like Muse or just want an open-ear way to listen to music and take phone calls, but Meta’s penchant for continually adding new features is, undoubtedly, going to be the highlight for everyone who ever buys them.

#10642. Employers, watch out for this trap when you lay people off

“We’re at-will. Just let them go.”

Leaders in the U.S. say these words, or something like them, with regularity. Because employment here is generally “at-will,” many assume they can terminate someone for any reason. But that misunderstands what at-will employment means—and what else is at play.

An employment decision doesn’t end when someone walks out the door. Even in at-will employment, every termination is judged in three courts: the court of law, the court of social media, and the court of public opinion. Each one can impact your business more than you realize.

The court of law

Despite what many people believe, at-will is not a magical shield against any legal liability. It doesn’t override other applicable laws, including those prohibiting discrimination, retaliation, or violations of whistleblower protections.

Most employees who leave an organization, even if they were fired, don’t sue their employer. But when they do, and if it gets to a trial, the question often isn’t whether the employer had the right to terminate them. It’s why they did.

Just ask the Society for Human Resource Management, the world’s largest HR association. In December 2025, a federal jury found SHRM liable for race discrimination and retaliation against a former employee. SHRM maintained that it followed appropriate procedures, even after the employee raised concerns of racial discrimination during her employment. But testimony and evidence at trial showed that the same individual who was responsible for investigating the employee’s complaints was also advising leaders on communications with her behind the scenes, and the employee’s termination paperwork had been drafted the same day she reported retaliation.

The jury awarded her $11.5 million. And the costs didn’t stop there.

In addition to the jury’s award and its own legal expenses, just this month, SHRM was ordered to pay more than $534,000 in attorneys’ fees for the plaintiff. Much like at-will employment, many leaders assume insurance covers everything. But SHRM’s insurer has sued to avoid paying $10 million of the verdict.

SHRM is appealing the decision. But regardless of the final outcome, it’s a reminder that employment decisions can carry significant costs in money, time, and reputation.

If it can happen to the organization that describes itself as “the global authority on work, workers, and the workplace,” it can happen to any employer.

The court of social media

Unlike a courtroom, social media doesn’t have rules of evidence or filing deadlines. There are headlines, screenshots, recordings, and sections that can shape public opinion in hours.

For many employees, a lawsuit feels intimidating and costly. Posting online does not. It feels—and is—accessible. A recorded layoff call, a screenshot of a termination email, or a “Day in the Life of Getting Fired from My Corporate Job” TikTok can reach more people in an hour than your organization reaches on LinkedIn all year.

By the time leaders start asking whether a recording is legal, it’s too late. People have made their conclusions, and continue to do so when you respond. While your lawyer may advise, “We don’t comment on personnel matters,” the public isn’t judging your legal defense. They’re evaluating whether your response reflects the values your organization claims to stand for.

After SHRM’s verdict, its CEO called it “just a blip in the history of SHRM.” That one word, “blip,” made headlines on its own.

Because in the court of social media, perception often shapes reality.

The court of public opinion

This court may have the smallest reach, but the longest memory.

One thing I learned as an employment lawyer and HR leader is that every employee is a walking billboard for your organization. People talk—to former colleagues, to friends, and to candidates, directly and on Glassdoor. And those people pay attention to what’s said, especially when a situation feels unfair.

The story spreads through their personal and professional communities. And there’s no formal appeal process in this court. Just your reputation is decided, one conversation at a time.

Use the 3-court test

None of this means that you can’t let someone go. You can, and sometimes that’s the best path, for your business and even that person. But it means that an employment decision—especially a termination—should be one that you’re comfortable defending in all three courts. Before you move forward, pause and ask:

  • Would it hold up in court? Look at the record: Did this person recently complain or take protected leave? Look at consistency: Are there others who’ve performed the same, or worse, and what happened to them? If a performance review says “Exceeds Expectations” but the termination notice says “Poor Performance,” that inconsistency won’t just concern the employee. It can raise real questions for a jury as well.
  • Would it survive a headline? Explain the decision in one sentence, as if someone who’s a complete stranger to your organization would read it. The decisions that are hardest to explain can be the ones most likely to go viral.
  • What will the team think? Not what an official statement says—what others will actually believe. Especially if the person leaving was a respected or vocal team member.

When you have doubts in any of these three areas, slow down and take a closer look.

When HR or Legal raises concerns, they’re usually not trying to create delays. They’re helping ensure the organization follows a process that is fair, defensible, and consistent.

The difference can be significant: between a fair process and Exhibit A.

A few extra days spent asking hard questions may prevent years of litigation, reputational damage, or rebuilding trust. Because at-will tells you what you’re allowed to do. It doesn’t tell you what you should do.

So, the next time someone in the room says, “We’re at-will,” ask the follow-up: “But would we win in all three courts?”

#10641. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

The builder estimates 50% to 60% of their AI work can now skip frontier models, running on two office circuits.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A lawyer posted on Reddit about their private AI server built from eight used 2018-era Nvidia Tesla V100 data center GPUs so case files never have to leave the office. With two 4-card SXM2 NVLink boards, four PEX switches, and SlimSAS cables everywhere — plus one burnt power connector — the builder now runs the open DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model with every expert in GPU memory, at up to 215 tokens per second. The four-GPU boards cost about $2,400 apiece when the builder bought them.

The eight Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB cards, each with 32GB of HBM2 at 900 GB/s, plug into SXM2, Nvidia’s mezzanine socket for data center GPUs, rather than PCIe slots, and are split across two baseboards. Inside each board, all four cards are NVLinked — NVLink is Nvidia’s direct GPU-to-GPU link — for 128GB per board, but the two boards only communicate over PCIe. Each board connects to the host through two PEX (PLX) switch cards over SlimSAS cables, four switches in all, with each switch handling two GPUs at PCIe 3.0 x8 speeds over its own x16 uplink.

The given prices are already in the past, though: used V100 SXM2 32GB cards are now listed on eBay for about $900, more than double the roughly $400 apiece from the post, and listings suggest prices are still climbing. The system also already has some other necessary components: a Gigabyte Threadripper Pro motherboard with a 12-core 3945WX CPU to match, 8x 32GB DDR4 RDIMM, one NUMA node, and two PSUs, 2,800 W in total, are on separate regular office circuits. This is a real-world case for used data center hardware as a cheap route to getting lots of fast VRAM together in one place.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is compressed to mostly 2 bits here, and its weights still total 248.8GB. The model’s “experts,” the parts that do most of the work for each word, live entirely in GPU memory, while about 110GB of lookup tables, called Engram tables, stay in the system’s regular RAM. Fetching from RAM costs about 0.12 milliseconds per step, which the builder says barely affects the speed numbers.

The first half of the model’s layers (0–19) runs on the first SXM2 board and the second half (20–39) on the second. Each board handles its heavy traffic over its own NVLink, so only one hand-off per step has to cross the slower PCIe link between the boards. In an earlier post, the builder found that splitting every layer across all eight cards made speeds “fall off a cliff” because of that PCIe hop.

Performance is surprisingly good for a model this size. Code comes out fastest, at up to 215 tokens per second, because a small draft model built into DeepSeek guesses five tokens ahead, and code is easy to guess. Legal writing, which is what the server is for, runs at up to 118 tokens per second.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Long documents take longer to get going: the model reads prompts at about 2,200 tokens per second, so at 128K tokens, the first token arrives after about a minute. It can accept up to 524K tokens of context. Three days before the post, the same model on four of these cards managed just 36–38 tokens per second. The jump came with the second board, which could presumably double performance under ideal circumstances, and the builder credits custom kernels and prefill work for the rest. See the table for the full breakdown.

Builder’s measurements, Nov. 5; greedy decoding, 1,024 tokens out, mean of two runs.

It wasn’t as simple as hooking everything up and turning on the power. The host reset itself twice with a fatal PCIe error on the link to one GPU board, both times with a higher power limit and uncapped GPU clocks. In this state, the cards drew 192–232 W, past the 180 W limit. The best guess, although “not proven,” is that a board stops responding during load spikes.

The resets stopped after the builder capped the clocks and removed one board whose power connector had a burn mark; “Check your connectors, people.” Each card is now capped at 150 W, half of its 300 W rating, with the graphics clock capped at 1522 MHz. A 200 W cap brought no appreciable performance gains, according to tests.

The system memory hit uncorrected ECC errors, too, which went away after the builder dropped the RAM from DDR4-3200 to DDR4-2666. One GPU was connected at x4 instead of x8 at last check, and the builder plans to reseat it; one commenter traced the same kind of problem on their own V100 to a bad cable.

The pain was worth the payoff as an estimated 50–60% of the lawyer’s existing LLM workflows can now run on the box instead of frontier models. Helping bridge the gap is a second DeepSeek server on two DGX Sparks, where the two systems hand work off to each other. The setup does appear to save money, at least when compared to API pricing, although the builder says it’s not really faster. However, it will protect client data “once it is self contained, which is the goal.”

The builder added that the V100 box might also get a 240 V circuit. Beyond power, the system is also on borrowed time with the Nvidia R580 driver branch, which is the last to support Volta. For now, the lawyer admits that it’s mostly a hobby, but in the future it may be a business idea. The next step is to handle two or three requests at once, something built and checked on a test system but not yet on the server.

#10638. The weird and brilliant innovations that led to electroconvulsive therapy—and the mystery of why it works

When I began considering electroconvulsive therapy, better known as electroshock, I assumed the “shock” part referred to the electrical zap you received. An electrode or two on your head. Some doctor pressing a button. A machine buzzed audibly. Zap, zap. You were shocked. Maybe changed forever. Maybe for good, maybe for ill. Zap, zap. Like a ray gun in a dystopian thriller. And no thriller was more dystopian (I flattered myself) than the anxious depression that had me in agony every waking moment.

Before I met those electrodes, accepted them onto my temples and into my life, my doctors gave me some books to read. I learned that most of what I thought I knew about ECT was deeply wrong. The real story was both grislier and more hopeful than you probably know. 

THE FIRST SHOCK TREATMENTS: FEVERS, INSULIN, AND ELECTROCUTED PIGS

When the Romanian-born psychiatrist Constance Pascal began using the term “shock” (choc) in her psychiatric clinic in France, around 1926, she was referring to physical treatments meant to surprise or disturb the body and brain, restoring the mind to equilibrium. Pascal considered mental illnesses to be a kind of allergic reaction, and she argued that resetting the brain and nervous system would be necessary for recovery. Pascal’s first shock therapies, in the late 1920s, used various means to prompt a reset, including induced fevers. Around the same time, in 1927 Berlin, the neurophysiologist Manfred Sakel was developing a new form of shock treatment in which a patient received potent injections of insulin. At proper doses, Sakel found he could induce a grand mal seizure as the patient came out of a hypoglycemic coma.

Insulin coma therapy produced astonishingly positive results for mood disorders—sometimes. (One famous recipient was the storied mathematician John Nash, who received insulin shocks for schizophrenia in 1961.) But results were markedly uneven. Ladislas Meduna, the Hungarian neuropathologist, shared Pascal’s interest in the possibilities of shock therapies and came to wonder whether seizures might offer a better route to healing.

In autopsies of epileptics, Meduna observed that the brains showed “tremendous changes” that were “just the opposite of those found in schizophrenia” (then a broad term that could encompass depression, schizoaffective disorders, and much more). In particular, Meduna noted that the glia—supportive cells sometimes called the janitors of the brain, whose duties include tending to our neurons—were overproduced in the brain tissue of epileptics, and vastly underrepresented in the cranial autopsies of patients with advanced mood disorders.

Pursuing this apparent antagonism between seizures and psychosis, Meduna introduced a new shock therapy in late 1934, injecting a catatonic patient with camphor, the compound then used in mothballs. Three weeks and five camphor-assisted seizures later, the patient was moving and talking—two things he hadn’t done in four years. Meduna repeated this apparent success with four subsequent patients, sometimes replacing camphor with the synthetic compound pentylenetetrazol, branded as Metrazol or Cardiazol, which achieved a similar convulsion but faster. It was also safer than insulin comas, which carried a real risk of death.

Still, Metrazol had severe drawbacks. One of the biggest was that the chemical seemed to induce feelings of absolute terror in patients before they finally fell into the coma. Not ideal for subjects already managing profound mental disturbances.

Meanwhile, in Italy, they were beginning to practice a new form of shocking the system, one that worked faster and more effectively than insulin or Metrazol—even if no one quite knew how it worked in the first place.

At the Clinic for Nervous and Mental Disorders in Rome, a little after 11 a.m. on April 11, 1938, the neurologist Ugo Cerletti placed a pair of electrodes on the temples of a man identified as “Enrico X.” Cerletti and his colleague, Lucio Bini, used a rubber band to hold the electrodes in place and electrocuted Enrico over a period of months, around 11 times. By the end of his electro-treatments, Signore X, the first ECT patient in history, was apparently recovered. The next month, in a presentation at the Royal Academy of Medicine in Rome, Cerletti and Bini administered an electro-treatment to a patient before an audience. In 1939, Cerletti and Bini coined a verb for what they’d invented: zapare, literally meaning “to zap.”

Even from the start, Cerletti was uneasy about the awesome power he commanded with those two electrodes. “When subjecting unconscious patients to such an extremely violent reaction as these convulsions, I had a sense of illicitness and felt as though I had somehow betrayed these patients,” he recalled later. Though Cerletti didn’t dwell on it, there was also the small matter of Enrico X’s relapse. He ended up readmitted to a psychiatric institution two years later.

Prehuman trials of electroconvulsions give a taste of the freewheeling sensibility that led to the development of electroshock. For example, in order to determine whether epilepsy affected the hippocampus, Cerletti as early as 1933 had sought to induce epilepsy in dogs. To do so he placed two electrodes on each dog, one inside the mouth, the other inside the rectum.

In Shock Therapy, their comprehensive 2007 history of ECT, Edward Shorter and David Healy report with dry understatement: “There was nothing innovative about this as such, and the mortality of the procedure was very high because the current passed through the dog’s heart, disrupting its electrical (pacemaker) activity.” It was an ignoble end for the dogs. For future experiments, Cerletti and Bini began placing the electrodes on a dog’s head, adequately producing a grand mal seizure.

Later, members of the Italian team visited a slaughterhouse in Rome, where dual-electrode stunning was used to render pigs unconscious before slaughter. Bini reported that after the shock, the stunned pigs reliably experienced grand mal seizures. This was precisely the seizure response that the clinicians sought in humans, and, barring extraordinarily high voltages, it carried no threat of death. (That came later, when the meat packers slit the pigs’ throats.)

ECT COMES OF AGE

Simply reading about dog rectums and pigs for slaughter, I quickly grasped the enduring stigma associated with ECT from these two details alone.

In a few of the books my doctors had recommended, I read how insulin, Metrazol, and ECT jockeyed for primacy during a period of remarkable change in neuropsychiatry, when physical treatments challenged and then overtook the formerly dominant psychoanalytic model. Then the beginning of World War II cut supply lines, making insulin prohibitively expensive or unavailable in some areas of the globe; ECT was cheaper, safer, and clinically far more attractive than either insulin or Metrazol. The war also emptied parts of Europe, notably Vienna, of many of its psychiatric eminences: Freud moved to England, Meduna went to Chicago, and the Berlin-born psychiatrist Lothar Kalinowsky, who worked on ECT in Rome under Cerletti, decamped to spread the electric gospel in London and then New York.

ECT, then, much like gin or the novel, was born in mainland Europe, refined in England, and naturalized in the States. Many American psychiatrists welcomed the practice. “Coming at a time when war is subjecting the population of the whole world to those intolerable mental strains that precipitate mental disease,” the Science News Letter wrote with excitement in 1940, “this new use of electricity for mental health instead of for death is being enthusiastically welcomed by the medical profession.”

That was the year ECT took America by storm. “In the summer of 1940, the East Coast must have literally buzzed with electricity,” Shorter and Healy write in Shock Therapy. And those who recovered often evangelized. The procedure involved some discombobulation, many patients said, perhaps some memory loss. But it had been undeniably worth it.

At least that was the case for the success stories. There were many others. The asylum era was still chugging along in the 1940s, and asylums were justly feared and hated. Among the inmates, ECT became one more blunt tool for asylum keepers to overuse, at a time when patients had precious few rights. As with fever therapy and hydrotherapy (repeated, prolonged, and often nonconsensual dousing), some asylum doctors in the 1940s and ’50s seem to have taken on ECT as a challenge: How much of this can my patients stand? Bini himself advanced an argument for the metodo dell’annichilimento, or “annihilation therapy,” which required zapping a patient multiple times a day. Other doctors picked up this method with the express purpose of rebuilding the patient’s personality from scratch.

These were tantalizing and terrifying things to read when I was deeply depressed and considering submitting to ECT myself.

THE MODERN, SOFTER SIDE OF ECT

My doctors told me that today’s ECT was quite different. No one was doing annihilation therapy in the U.S. anymore, one said. Plus, modern or “modified” ECT was much more civilized because the electrical pulses were briefer and more targeted, and the doctors gave you anesthesia and muscle relaxers and even an oxygen tube to prevent asphyxia. All the horror stories, my psychiatrist said, dated from the era of “unmodified” ECT. “We’re past the grisly stuff now,” he told me.

But that didn’t make the history any easier to read.

Yes, anesthesia and tranquilizers entered the picture—particularly in 1951, with the introduction of the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, still used in ECT today. But many asylums and hospitals were slow to adopt these new, gentler practices. According to the science journalist and ECT skeptic Robert Whitaker, more than 1 million patients got forced ECT in the 1940s and ’50s. Even kids didn’t escape the electrodes. From 1942 to 1947, Bellevue Hospital in New York treated 98 children, some as young as 4, with a long sequence of ECT treatments.

My heart rate slowed a bit when I read about the softer side of ECT. It’s considered sufficiently gentle to be offered as a first resort for elderly patients who can’t tolerate SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) or other pharmacological interventions. I was even more surprised to learn that ECT didn’t attain its stigma—its association with persecution and alleged brain damage—until the mid-1960s, thanks in part to emerging psychopharmaceuticals but mainly amid a frantic new campaign to abolish ECT.

THE CAMPAIGN AGAINST ECT

The antipsychiatry movement was a coalition between heterodox psychiatrists and members of the New Left. It emerged at a time when the antiauthoritarian ethos of young baby boomers came into conflict with a procedure that recalled the tyranny of asylum medicine. “Shock resonated because, like nuclear energy, [ECT] had the aura of an out-of-control technology imposed by an authoritarian society,” observed the journalist Larry Tye, who, with Kitty Dukakis, authored an illuminating 2006 book about electroshock. By the 1970s, Tye reported, detractors had begun “picket[ing] outside electroshock clinics with signs linking the practitioners to Spanish inquisitor Tomás de Torquemada and Nazi executioner Adolf Eichmann.” The anti-ECT campaign has been vigorous and well funded, thanks not least to munificent contributions from the Church of Scientology, which has also played a central role in organizing.

Accordingly, ECT therapy was severely curtailed in most parts of the country. Numbers are tricky, as there’s no central trove of data, but the most plausible estimate is that the yearly number of ECT patients in the U.S. fell from around 300,000 in the 1950s and ’60s to around 59,000 by 1975; by 1980, that number had dropped further, to around 32,000. “It is as though penicillin had suddenly gone into a decline in the absence of any objective circumstance that might discourage physicians from prescribing it or patients from accepting it,” Shorter and Healy wrote.

One can understand the skepticism. I know I did. But as I read about the campaign to expunge ECT, I wondered whether the problem was a failure to distinguish the baby from the bathwater. It seems statistically undeniable that, during ECT’s period in the wilderness, millions of depressed or bipolar or schizophrenic Americans were functionally denied recourse to ECT. One doctor told me we’d never know how many died because ECT was drummed out of so many American hospitals. ECT’s frequently lurid portrayals in popular culture only bolstered the eye-popping claims of the antipsychiatry camp: ECT turns you into a zombie; it erases your entire memory; it will literally break your back.

I found a few books that mounted a defense of ECT. Sometimes half-apologetic, other times closer to triumphant. I read the Shorter and Healy history, Carrie Fisher’s memoir about electroshock, and Tye’s book with Dukakis, entitled Shock: The Healing Power of Electroconvulsive Therapy. (“In some ways ECT is less traumatic for me than going to the dentist, and certainly less frightening than the root canal,” Dukakis wrote.)

But when I tried to find some authoritative consensus about memory loss, I kept meeting a chorus of contradiction from the medical literature. Some doctors said memory loss would be mild; others said it could be “more pronounced” (than what?); but the third and loudest group said that memory loss was a canard, a talking point for antipsychiatrists, adding that most patients reported few to no cognitive problems. When I went online to eavesdrop on patient forums, the consensus was clearer: Memory loss is very, very real.

I’m only speculating here, but I do wonder whether, in their zeal to defend a lifesaving treatment from demagogic skeptics, some ECT advocates may have pushed back with their own immoderate claims. Whatever the cause, it’s a strange experience to have different doctors tell you different things about what’s about to happen to your memory. It’s even stranger when, after a few treatments, you can’t quite remember which doctor told you what.

GENERATING NEW NEURONS (AND OFTEN HOPE)

The most baffling, endlessly intriguing questions about ECT are how and why it works. Physicians since ancient times have recorded the sometimes salutary effects of seizures on certain forms of mental illness, yet even today we don’t know precisely why a given brain is happier, or clearer, or calmer, following a few seizures. There’s an old saw comparing ECT to aspirin: We don’t know how it works, but it works magnificently. Still, a few general ideas about the mechanism of ECT are widely accepted.

During the seizure, affected neurons all fire at the same time, several times per second. Some doctors refer to this effect as the brain “resetting” itself. As a result of this firing, the brain releases a welcome surplus of neurohormones such as norepinephrine and neurotransmitters such as dopamine. The most intriguing recent account for ECT’s high rate of response—often reported at around 75% to 80% for major depressives who’ve failed to find relief with pharmacology—is that the release of these brain chemicals can stimulate neural growth across various regions of the brain. Per brain imaging, just a few ECT treatments are often enough to spur visible volume increases in multiple cortical regions, not least in the hippocampus, the area of the brain that is prey to atrophy during major depression and other maladies, including addiction, certain schizoaffective disorders, dementia, and Alzheimer’s.

ECT’s demonstrated neurogenetic properties offer a compelling explanation for why the treatment remains a most effective antidepressant. That the brain grows and shows markedly more, and more regular, activity after ECT treatment is potentially confusing to lay­ people, many of whom take the treatment to be inherently damaging—­“scarring” is the preferred participle among the skeptics, as though doctors have applied a knife or a white-hot poker to your brain. Of course, surprisingly little electricity goes through you; not enough to singe or scar. Comparisons are tricky, because the human machine and, say, the refrigerator require different currents, but the amount of energy that zaps you during a single ECT session is mercifully modest—perhaps the equivalent of charging your phone by 1% or powering a lightbulb for a few seconds.

Discoveries about hippocampal growth after ECT are straightforwardly exciting. For those of us who grew up in the 1980s and ’90s, the essential unrecuperability of brain cells and memories was treated as a basic fact in “just say no”–style antidrug campaigns and even biology class. That was all wrong, even then. Neurogenesis had been established in small mammals and birds by the 1980s, while in the 1990s, we discovered that the human brain has its own stem cells—pluripotent little guys that can become new neurons, sometimes creating new connections that support neuroplasticity, as well as fresh glial cells to clean and maintain the brain’s circuits.

Still, certain disagreements persist. Some of the keenest students and proponents of ECT believe the seizure is the crucial mechanism, while other experts argue it’s the body’s postseizure response that hits the reset button, rather than the seizure itself. If the latter group is right, that opens the intriguing possibility that future advances in brain imaging and brain stimulation might reveal a gentler shortcut toward triggering an anticonvulsive response, hypergenerating these chemicals, and reinvigorating the hippocampus and its neighbors, all without the dreaded seizure.

Regardless, ECT remains the nuclear power of psychiatric treatment: much maligned, often misused, yet sturdy and powerful, the gold standard that we’ve somehow disowned. Among latter-day electrical treatments, which include transcranial magnetic stimulation and vagus nerve stimulation, none thus far has shown the efficacy of modern ECT. Particularly for acute cases—people who might not have the time to wait for another drug to work or not to work—ECT is unmatched.

It could also be on the verge of becoming much more effective. Cutting-edge research into ultrabrief pulses and hypertargeted forms of the treatment offer the tantalizing possibility that future patients might receive greater benefits with fewer side effects. But we’re not there yet.

There are, of course, legitimate lines of skepticism. Some skeptics raise reasonable methodological points. For example, while we can draw on various controlled trials into ECT’s efficacy, placebo-controlled trials—in which a control group undergoes a sham version of the treatment—are rare, largely because they raise major ethical concerns. (Fooling a depressive into thinking he’s had a seizure is both tricky and mean.)

The other major concerns involve consent and side effects. In the U.K., for example, there are complaints that some older patients, especially women, have received ECT against their will, and that doctors have minimized side effects, leaving patients shaken when they discover unexpected memory deficits.

Today, the anti-ECT movement is gaining ground again. In the U.S., opponents have once again taken to the courts, where litigation over undisclosed risks helped push one manufacturer of ECT machines into bankruptcy in 2021. A separate lawsuit produced a 2026 settlement from two psychiatrists accused of understating potential harms.

As a journalist rather than a researcher, all I can say with certainty is what I’ve seen empirically in myself and other patients: ECT can have miraculous-seeming positive effects for the deeply depressed. It also verifiably inhibits the consolidation of more recent memories. My treatment was voluntary, and I lost access to more of the previous months than I’d been prepared for. What I got in exchange, though, was real healing; slow at first, then undeniable. Without ECT, I could’ve harmed myself and continued courting death. Instead, I returned to life in all its mess and splendor. Historically, ECT has indeed been much abused. But among the many ways to abuse ECT is withholding it from a patient whose life it could save.

Excerpted from Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness by Ted Scheinman. Published by Simon & Schuster. Copyright © 2026 by Ted Scheinman. All rights reserved.

#10636. Adobe’s SVP of design believes it’s a golden age of design. Hear him out

It’s never been easier to make an image. Even for people who don’t consider themselves creative, translating an idea into an illustration, graphic, video—any format, really—is now as simple as typing a prompt into a box (quality not guaranteed). 

Adobe knows this. The company, which has long been the tool of choice for professional creatives, is now looking to “aggressively acquire the next generation of Adobe loyalists,” as the outgoing CEO, Shantanu Narayen, put it during a recent earnings call. That means bringing the not-so-creative among us into the fold with tools like Firefly AI and Adobe Express. Even its professional-grade tools are eyeing novice creatives with AI agents that make navigating complex tools easier.

The strategy appears to be working. So far this year, Adobe has increased the number of “Creative freemium” users—people using free versions of Firefly and Adobe Express—by 70%, reaching 100 million monthly active users. Meanwhile, its professional-focused business remains healthy and growing, though at a slower rate (15% year over year as of Q3).

As Adobe kicks off its biggest event of the year with its Adobe Max conference, Fast Company spoke with Eric Snowden, Adobe’s SVP of design, about what this push into freemium means for the way his team thinks about designing tools, the challenges of bringing Adobe products into third-party apps like ChatGPT, and why this might truly be the most exciting time to be a designer. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Fast Company: For the last few years, Adobe has really pushed its identity as a company that makes creative tools for everyone—not just professional designers, but also people who don’t necessarily consider themselves designers at all. I’d love to understand what the business imperative for that broader definition of a creator is to you and Adobe more broadly.

Eric Snowden: I think this has been a trend for Adobe for longer than the last few years. I mean, if you go back and look at things like Elements and other products, we’ve been trying to bring creativity to more and more people for many years. And I think between technology that’s come up—mobile and now AI—we can just go broader and broader than we’ve ever been able to do before. Adobe’s really been about empowering people to express themselves and to communicate in new ways. And that’s been at the core of our company’s mission for a long time. We’re just able to do that in ways we haven’t been able to do before.

I think it’s been accelerated, but I don’t know that it’s a completely new thing for us. And I think you’re seeing more and more people want to do this, right? I think whether it’s through social media or other forums, people want to express themselves in new ways, and they’ve got new forums to do that. And so, as demand has grown, I think we’ve really wanted to meet that demand for a broader audience.

Back in June, your outgoing CEO said, “We believe now is the time to aggressively acquire the next generation of Adobe loyalists.” And to just kind of push that idea a little bit more, why is that so important?

We have an easier on-ramp now than we’ve ever had before. I think whether it’s products like Express that anyone can pick up and use, or it’s the new technology, like agents or other things we brought into our flagship tools, . . . it’s just easier to be creative than it’s ever been.

I started using Adobe products when I was a teenager. I’ve always been a big believer that people pick their first creative tools when they’re really young, and we have a lot of data around that. . . . Maybe they become a creative, and maybe they don’t. But it’s something that people start pretty young, and so we want to make sure that we’ve got a really great on-ramp for folks who want to be creative.

For me, it was creating posters and websites for the band I was in, and I didn’t know that was going to lead me into being the SVP of design at Adobe. I didn’t even know design was a career at that point, but I think that on-ramp exposed me to this entire world that I didn’t know existed.

Obviously the on-ramp that you experienced is very different from the on-ramp a 14-year-old might experience today. How would you characterize that difference? How are you trying to reach that younger generation of potential creative?

There are so many different ways. One is, where they can express themselves is extremely different. I didn’t have social networks or other places to express myself. I think that’s a big part of it. At the time, we only had high-end professional specialist tools, and so I was using Photoshop to make a poster for a band that felt a little bit like taking a 747 to go to the grocery store. It was just overkill for what I needed. I think today I might have used something like Adobe Express to do that, but that could have introduced me in a much easier way and an on-ramp to the things I need today. 

But I also love the approach we’re taking with agents inside of our professional tools, because it feels like a guide that can bring you into something like Photoshop or even After Effects. I was playing with the After Effects agent a week or so ago, and the beauty of it is you can prompt your way into the product, but under the hood, it is still After Effects. I liken it to a self-driving car where it’s doing its thing, but at any moment you can drive the wheel and you have full control. It’s got all of the layers and all the keyframes and the easings and everything underneath it, so at any moment where you want to get in and tweak every knob and dial, that’s there for you. 

Most of us at Adobe, we think a lot about how we learned Adobe’s products and how we can make that easier. That’s something that has stuck in my head for the entirety of my time at Adobe. And I think a lot about how we make it easier for someone to learn these tools than it was for me, because the ceiling is so high in these tools, which is the beauty of them. But we want to make that first step or two into them as seamless and as low as possible.

So what does that look like? Can you give me a good example of how you’ve made the accessibility clear?

Yeah, one of the things I just mentioned, right? Bringing agents into our tools, I think, is one way. Another way is, there are brand new tools that are easier to pick up that are specialized. So, something like using Adobe Fresco on the iPad for drawing. It’s on a specialized device that is great for working in that way. It’s a tool that is dedicated for that use case. There are also things in our flagship tools. Like one example I always give is the properties panel in Illustrator, and this is getting a little nerdy, but we took all of these different panels and combined them into a single panel, right? We didn’t take away anything. All those other panels already exist, but we gave people a single place to access most of the things they need, and that just simplifies getting to know a product when you come in for the first time. But it actually doesn’t take anything away from our power users.

One of the the fun, but also really hard, tensions of this job is: How do you change things in our existing tools to make it easier for new people to onboard without disrupting the fact that professionals have very specific, bespoke workflows that if you change a a pixel or two, you can really throw them off of their game. It’s like it’s a musical instrument to them. You can’t move the keys on a keyboard—it’s the same thing, and so I think it’s about finding that balance. And so it’s something we’re thinking about all the time, like across the portfolio.

I would love to understand how your team designs a single product for someone who has never opened Photoshop, let’s say, and for someone who’s used it for like 20 years, right? Are those two different products in your mind? Two different experiences?

I’m glad you brought that up as an example because we recently launched this AI-assisted mode in Photoshop, and I think the goal with that is to have a dedicated place that people can land who have never used Photoshop before. It’s very simplified; an AI-centric experience, like a workspace where they can go in and they can prompt their way to editing their image, but they are still in the context of Photoshop. It is one click away to get the more full-featured interface, and there’s sort of this interplay between the two where they can graduate from this simple interface into the full interface. 

Now they don’t have to do that, right? They could have a full editing experience in this simplified interface, and people can go from the more complex interface into the simplified one if they wanted to. But I think it’s about bringing them into the entire tool, giving them an experience that you know. Again, it’s about that first step or two. It’s like: What is that day one experience like, and giving them something they feel like they can digest and they get a result that they’re proud of as quickly as possible. 

I was a Photoshop teacher at Parsons [School of Design] for a number of years, and when I was teaching Photoshop, it was really about how do I spend the least amount of time possible to get someone to have an image that comes out the other end that they feel proud of. Because once they did that, they were willing to invest the time to learn the breadth and depth of one of the most powerful pieces of software on the planet. You can do anything in Photoshop. That’s the beauty of it. And so it’s about how do we give them that success as quickly as possible, and then we sort of guide them through the rest of it and show them the depth of this kind of amazing tool.

Earlier this year Jesus Diaz wrote about how Adobe is rolling out a new integration for ChatGPT, which effectively lets users, @ Adobe in ChatGPT’s interface, and then use natural language to accomplish whatever it is they want to accomplish, pulling from the capabilities from across Creative Cloud apps. 

What was interesting to me about that announcement was that it was sort of an acknowledgement that many of the people who are new to Adobe products are not going to use them in the same way, or onboard in the same way, that you all are accustomed to. As someone who is designing these products, I’m curious what challenges it creates for you and your team when somebody has access to Creative Cloud through third-party apps like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini?

We think a lot about continuity across experiences because, to your point, there will be some people that are introduced to it through ChatGPT, and then do experience it through our flagship applications. We want to make sure they have an experience that doesn’t feel like they have to start over when they come into our products. We talk a lot about skills transfers—this idea that if they build a skill in one place and they go to a second place, that skill is something that was a good investment for them that they can build on top of. We want to make sure that the pieces of the interface that we bring into these third parties, as they learn those, those things are valuable to them as they progress. 

We also realize there will be some people that will stay in ChatGPT. There will be some people that go the other direction—people who are using our flagship tools and then find it in ChatGPT want to make sure the skills transfer goes the other way. And so that continuity of experience is one part of it. But I think the most important thing, and the thing that is unique about Adobe’s approach to all of this, is we’re a workflow company. People aren’t usually coming to us to use a single feature, a single product. They are trying to accomplish a goal, and they are often using a product or a couple of products to accomplish something much larger.

And so we need to make sure that all of this stuff works together, whether it’s a couple of Adobe tools or an Adobe tool and a third-party tool. Because as a workflow company, that’s what people expect from us and often come to us for. That can be a challenge when you don’t control the full end to end, but that’s something we’re really trying to make sure we get right for our customers.

Talking about the freemium model, your freemium monthly active users have increased a lot over the past year. How does that change the way that you think about designing Adobe’s products? And how are you thinking about graduating them into a paid tier? 

Yeah, it’s interesting. I think it goes back to the previous challenge of new users, and they’re tied together, even though freemium doesn’t always equate to new. But it is about giving people value and feeling an accomplishment as soon as possible. And in a freemium model, you’re allowed to give them that without having to have a sign-in or a paywall be the first thing that someone experiences.  

When people think of Photoshop, they do think of this sort of unlimited potential, but they still don’t even know what is possible with Photoshop. And so, the more we can show them what these tools are capable of, the more we can get them excited. And I think in these new models, we’re allowed to show them more of that before we ask them to sign up or to pay for something. That is beneficial to Adobe, right? We can show them like the magic that we can give to them; that’s really exciting to be able to show versus tell, and I think the freemium model allows us to do more of that. 

It’s a real value exchange with a customer. At some point, we’re saying, ‘give us either your email or your money,’ and it’s clear what value we’re exchanging with them. And I think doing that at the right time, that’s when conversion happens. If you’re doing that at the wrong time, I think that makes conversion more difficult. That is a design challenge to figure out, when does that handshake happen? I think you get the best conversion numbers where there’s the right there’s the right balance. If you have it too far on one side, the user feels like they haven’t gotten enough to warrant whatever you’re asking them to do. And if it’s too far on the other side, that’s not good for the business. And so I think it’s about finding that right balance where everyone benefits from that exchange.

It’s an interesting time to be talking about this with the Canva news [last] week, with the company laying off or restructuring around 22% of its workforce. Part of those pressures, it seems, comes from the pressures of building a product that caters to a very large base of people who use the tool for free, but are also using very compute-intensive features. Obviously, Adobe has a different business model. You’re a completely different company—this is not apples to apples. But I’m curious because we’re here: What did that news reveal to you? 

Yeah, it’s. I mean, it’s an interesting question. I mean, obviously we saw that news, but you know, I frankly try not to think about that too much. Canva’s doing interesting things out there, but I think we have to keep focused on what we’re doing, and I think we are doing something very different. I think we are a very different company. I mean, to your point, creativity is a piece of our business, but we have other massive lines of business that are connected to creativity. But they do one thing, and we do a multitude of things, and we do a multitude of things that are all interconnected. And so, it’s just kind of hard to make that comparison in a lot of ways.

One thing that I wanted to talk about is a data point that you all came up with in a survey from back in the summer about small business owners and creative marketing. It says the average small business owner fills five roles a day, adding up to 200 extra hours a year; 44% act as their own marketer; 41% act as social media manager, and 35% as creative director. 

Those are pretty crazy numbers. It makes total sense to me that that’s the case, but just seeing the numbers kind of blows my mind. When did you all suspect this shift was happening,? Is this an AI-enabled change in the way that people run their businesses?

This shift has been happening for a while, but I think it’s been nearly impossible for people to keep up with this. Just the burden that’s put on these businesses, it’s pretty wild, and I think AI could be part of the solution to that.

But the demands and expectations on small businesses are also echoed in enterprises and everything else. Like the demand for content is at an all-time high, and it is growing. There’s just insane expectations for all these different channels . . . it just keeps scaling, keeps getting bigger and bigger. And I think that’s where the opportunity for us is to help, whether it’s tools like Express, where people can do some of this stuff themselves if they need to; whether it’s through agents; whether it’s through empowering professionals to do this work faster and better.

Our industry focuses a lot about productivity with AI, but we don’t talk enough about the fact that there are things that we can do now that we could not do before. Yes, all of us are being asked to do more, and yes, everybody’s being asked to work faster. But my team talks a lot about, what can we do now that we couldn’t do six months ago? The fact that we can build our own tools and our own plugins, or the fact that people who couldn’t do motion graphics can add that to their toolkit. I mean I think it’s really about not just the productivity part of AI, but raising the ceiling on either the breadth of work people can do, or the quality of work people can do. I think it’s about finding the balance between those two things in a lot of ways.

Your team can do things that it wasn’t able to do six months ago. Any thoughts on what you’d like to be able to do in six months that you can’t do now?

When it comes to my team in particular, I know there’s a lot of concern in the design community about what it means to be a product designer. I think that’s fair because the world is changing, and we all have to acknowledge that. But when I talk to my team, I think this is actually one of the most exciting times to be a product designer. In the past, if you were a designer and you had an idea that you were passionate about, you would have to convince someone to build that idea. Either find an engineering friend or a partner who was up for it, and convince them to help build a prototype with you, or convince a product manager who controlled engineering resources that this was a good idea. 

You don’t really need to do that anymore. You can just build it yourself. I know people are founding companies where it’s a bunch of designers and a single engineer, and I think the power that designers have to go just do things on their own is unprecedented, and I mean that literally. I think as time goes on, that is going to just get greater. And so, if you project six months into the future, what people can build is going to be amazing.

I would say a good portion of the software that I run on my computer these days, whether it’s Photoshop plug-ins I built, or software that I’m using to to make myself more productive, I’ve written myself; bespoke things for me that is running alongside Adobe software that I use or connected to it to make myself more productive. That’s a really interesting world that we’re entering into, and I can see that accelerating. For product designers who really embrace that, that is an exciting new world, but it is a very different world than the one we’re living in today, or certainly one we’ve lived in historically. I think if people lean into that, there’s something really fascinating and interesting there—and fun.

I think we should occasionally talk about the fact that as a designer, being able to just build stuff is really fun. It reminds me of the Flash days of the internet where anything felt possible, and I haven’t felt that way in a long time.
